deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page defines 𝔉x = ∫_0^x (e^t−1)/t dt = Σ_{n≥1} x^n/(n·n!) (in modern terms −Ein(−x) = Ei(x) − log x − γ), with values such as 𝔉i and 𝔉2i. On this page Fx is evidently that function. The next page is dated Oct. 1812, so this page is probably from about 1812.

(1) Power sums. 𝔉 has the trivial zero x = 0. Remove it: φ(x) = 𝔉(x)/x = 1 + a1 x + a2 x^2 + ... with a_k = 1/((k+1)(k+1)!). So a1 = 1/4, a2 = 1/18, a3 = 1/96, a4 = 1/600, a5 = 1/4320, ...

The listed sums are small, while the roots have modulus about 7.6, so the r must be the reciprocals 1/ρ of the nonzero roots ρ. This identification is mine, but every check confirms it.

Newton's identities for p_k = Σ r^k (my reconstruction of the implicit step) are:
- p1 = −a1
- p_k = −(a1 p_{k−1} + ... + a_{k−1} p1) − k a_k

Equivalently, p_k = −k·[x^k] log φ(x). They give:
- p1 = −1/4
- p2 = 1/16 − 1/9 = −7/144 = −(1/4)^2·7/9
- p3 = 7/576 + 1/72 − 1/32 = −1/192 = −(1/4)^3·1/3
- p4 = −31/518400 = −(1/4)^4·31/2025
- p5 = 29/414720 = +(1/4)^5·29/405

Gauss continues in the same way to p15. He factors out (1/4)^k throughout. The value 54068269/43762690125 was first written on the Σr^9 line, struck out, and moved to Σr^10; Σr^9 then received 94519/22325625.

(2) Roots. 'Hieraus folgen die Wurzeln' ('From this follow the roots'). For large k, p_k is dominated by the smallest root pair: p_k ≈ 2|ρ1|^{−k} cos(kφ1). The modulus and argument can therefore be extracted from consecutive power sums. This is Bernoulli's method in Euler's power-sum form, e.g. via p_{k+2} − 2Re(r)p_{k+1} + |r|^2 p_k ≈ 0.

Gauss obtains:
- ρ1 = 3.183297 ± 6.8964441 i, with log10|ρ1| = 0.8807003 and φ = 65°12'20.8''.
- A second, rougher pair 3.796 ± 13.296 i, with log r = 1.14432 and φ = 73(4?)°39'45''.

My checks:
- Asymptotic check of the first pair. For Im z > 0, Ei(z) ~ (e^z/z)(1 + 1/z + 2/z^2 + ...) + iπ, so zeros satisfy (e^z/z)S(z) ≈ log z + γ − iπ. At z = 3.1833 + 6.8964i the left side ≈ 2.585 − 1.993i and the right side ≈ 2.605 − 2.004i. This agrees within the accuracy of the asymptotic series.
- Dominance check: 2·7.5957^{−15}·cos(15·65.22°) ≈ −2.51e−14. Gauss's p15 = −(1/4)^15·953612037463/34945602132065625 ≈ −2.54e−14.
- Second pair: fixed-point iteration on the asymptotic equation gives z ≈ 3.936 + 13.401i, i.e. |z| ≈ 13.97 (log ≈ 1.1451) and arg ≈ 73.6°. This matches Gauss's polar values log r = 1.14432 and φ ≈ 73°40' well. It does not match his rectangular 3.796 + 13.296i, which corresponds to |z| = 13.83 and arg ≈ 74.1°.
errors: Σr = −1/4 is only the formal Newton value −a1. 𝔉(x)/x has order 1, so its Hadamard product carries an exponential factor e^{Bx}. The genuine (conjugate-paired) sum Σ1/ρ need not equal −1/4. The values for k ≥ 2 are unaffected because they converge absolutely.
The second root is written 3.183296 − 6.8964441 i but the first is 3.183297 + 6.8964441 i. This is a trivial last-digit inconsistency for a conjugate pair.

For the first root, the rectangular and polar forms disagree slightly. From 3.183297 + 6.8964441i one gets log10 r = 0.88057 and φ ≈ 65°13'22'', against Gauss's 0.8807003 and 65°12'20.8'' (about a 1' discrepancy). The two forms probably come from different stages of refinement.

For the second pair, the rectangular values 3.796 ± 13.296i are inconsistent with the stated polar values (log r = 1.14432, φ ≈ 73°39'45''). The polar values agree with my independent estimate z ≈ 3.93 + 13.40i, so the rectangular numbers are an earlier, cruder approximation.
The higher power sums (k = 6…15) have not been individually verified here. The order of magnitude and sign of p15 agree with the dominant-root asymptotics.

results.what: Power sums of the reciprocal zeros of 𝔉(x)/x = Σ x^{n−1}/(n·n!) (the entire exponential integral), computed exactly by Newton's identities up to k = 15
results.modern_name: Newton–Girard identities applied to a transcendental entire function (Euler's method of power sums of reciprocal zeros)
results.usually_credited_to: Newton (identities); Euler (application to transcendental equations, e.g. zeros of Bessel-type series)

results.what: First complex zeros of 𝔉(x) = Ei(x) − log x − γ (equivalently, zeros of Ein at −z): z ≈ 3.1833 ± 6.8964 i and roughly 3.93 ± 13.40 i
results.modern_name: Complex zeros of the entire exponential integral Ein(z) / of Ei(z) − log z − γ
results.usually_credited_to: Numerical tabulation of exponential-integral zeros is generally 20th-century; no specific early attribution known to me

results.what: Extraction of the dominant complex-conjugate root pair from high-order power sums
results.modern_name: Bernoulli's method / Euler power-sum method for dominant roots (precursor of the Graeffe–Dandelin–Lobachevsky approach)

deep.surprise_reason: The method (Newton sums plus dominant-root extraction) was standard Euler-era technique. Applying it to locate complex zeros of the exponential integral around 1812, with several correct digits, is a pleasant unpublished numerical result. The zeros of Ein/Ei − log − γ are not usually associated with Gauss, but this is a numerical computation rather than a new theorem.
